text: Miriam Amanda "Ma" Ferguson (née Wallace; June 13, 1875 – June 25, 1961) was an American politician who served two non-consecutive terms as governor of Texas: from 1925 to 1927 and from 1933 to 1935. She was the first female governor of Texas and the second woman elected to the governorship of any U.S. state to assume office, after Nellie Tayloe Ross of Wyoming. Born in Bell County, Texas, she studied at Salado College and Baylor Female College. At age 24, she married James Edward Ferguson, a lawyer, at her father's farm near Belton in Bell County. Her nickname "Ma" came from her initials "M. A." and the fact that her husband was known as "Pa" Ferguson; they had two daughters, Ouida Wallace Ferguson and Dorrace Watt Ferguson. James Ferguson served as governor from 1915 to 1917, and during his second term, he was investigated by State Attorney General Dan Moody for actions against the University of Texas. The Texas State Senate impeached him, convicted him on ten charges, and barred him from holding state office again. After his impeachment, Ma Ferguson ran in the Democratic primary for governor and won, with open support from her husband, whom she said she would consult for advice. She ran in the 1924 general election, promoting the slogan "two governors for the price of one," and her speeches involved introducing her husband and letting him take the platform. A common campaign slogan was "Me for Ma, and I Ain't Got a Durned Thing Against Pa." Patricia Bernstein of the Houston Chronicle noted that it was never in doubt who was really running things during her tenure. After winning the primary, she defeated George C. Butte, a prominent lawyer and University of Texas dean, who was the strongest Republican nominee since Reconstruction. Due to her husband's corruption and impeachment, thousands of voters crossed party lines, and Butte won nearly 300,000 votes—many from women and suffragists—though Ferguson still won 422,563 votes (58.9%) to Butte's 294,920 (41.1%). Butte had been supported by former governor William P. Hobby, who succeeded James Ferguson in 1917 and won a full term in 1918. In 1924, Ma Ferguson became the first elected female chief executive of Texas, the second elected female state governor in the U.S. to assume office, and the first to be elected in a general election. Nellie Tayloe Ross had been sworn in to finish her late husband’s unexpired term two weeks before Ferguson’s inauguration, though both won their elections on the same day. Ferguson’s campaign manager was Homer T. Brannon of Fort Worth. In 1926, state attorney general Dan Moody, who had investigated her husband and recovered $1 million for Texas citizens, defeated her in a run-off election, becoming the next and youngest governor of Texas. Suffragist activism played a major role in her defeat, as these women rallied behind Moody. Ferguson ran again in 1932, narrowly winning the Democratic nomination over incumbent Ross S. Sterling, and then soundly defeating Republican Orville Bullington in the general election, 521,395 (61.6%) to 322,589 (38.1%). It was a year of Democratic successes as Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president. Bullington, a cousin of the first wife of John G. Tower, performed better than most Texas Republican candidates but did not match Butte’s 1924 showing. Her second term was less controversial than her first; rumors circulated that state highway contracts went only to companies that advertised in the Fergusons' newspaper, the Ferguson Forum, but a House committee investigated and no charges were filed. The Great Depression led to cuts in state and federal funding, reducing the number of commissioned officers in the Texas Rangers to 45 and limiting their transportation to free railroad passes or personal horses. In 1932, the Rangers supported Governor Ross Sterling in his re-election bid over "Ma" Ferguson, prompting her to immediately discharge all serving Rangers upon taking office in January 1933. The force’s salaries and funding were slashed, and its size was reduced to 32 men. This disorganization allowed Texas to become a haven for Depression-era gangsters such as Bonnie and Clyde, George "Machine Gun" Kelly, Pretty Boy Floyd, and Raymond Hamilton. The hasty appointment of unqualified Rangers proved ineffective. The legislature, convinced by the disorganization, hired a Chicago-based consulting firm, which concluded that Texas had extremely high criminality and underfunded, undermanned, loose, and obsolete law enforcement. The consultants recommended merging the Rangers with the Texas Highway Patrol to form the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS). After deliberation, the legislature approved the plan, and the resolution creating the DPS was passed in 1935 under Governor James V. Allred, with an initial budget of $450,000, making the DPS operational on August 10. In October 1933, Ferguson signed Texas House Bill 194, which helped establish the University of Houston as a four-year institution. "Fergusonism," the Fergusons' brand of populism, remains controversial in Texas. As governor, she addressed key issues, aligning with "wets" in the prohibition debate despite being a teetotaler like her husband, and opposing the Ku Klux Klan, which declined after 1925 due to a national scandal involving its president, D. C. Stephenson. She is described as a fiscal conservative but also supported a state sales tax and corporate income tax. She is often credited with a quote allegedly about bilingualism in Texas schools: "If English was good enough for Jesus Christ, it ought to be good enough for the children of Texas," though variations of this statement date back to 1881 and were used to ridicule certain Christians; Ferguson did not originate it. During her two non-consecutive terms, she issued almost 4,000 pardons, many to those convicted of violating prohibition laws. In 1930, Secretary of State Jane Y. McCallum published a pamphlet criticizing her pardons. Though never proven, rumors persisted that pardons were available in exchange for cash payments to her husband. In 1936, voters passed a constitutional amendment removing the governor’s power to issue pardons and transferring it to a politically independent Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles. Several labor laws were passed during her two terms. In a 1932 speech, her husband James E. Ferguson defended "Fergusonism," citing reforms such as child labor laws, workmen's compensation, aid for rural education, a free textbook law, and regulations on women’s working hours. Miriam Ferguson herself defended "Fergusonism," citing liberal measures like a semi-monthly pay day law, an eight-hour workday, the establishment of an Industrial Accident Board, and the creation of the Lower Colorado and Brazos River Authorities. Except for an unsuccessful bid to replace Governor W. Lee "Pappy" O'Daniel in 1940, the Fergusons remained retired after 1935. In that 1940 campaign, Ma Ferguson trailed O'Daniel’s main rival, Ernest O. Thompson of Amarillo, who was Texas Railroad Commissioner. Her husband James died of a stroke in 1944, and Miriam Ferguson died of congestive heart failure in 1961 at age 86. She was buried in the Texas State Cemetery in Austin.
